I was all geared up to talk about how this is an example of series 1 stuff trying towards more narrative focus, rather than just "weird thing kill pplz," then I found out it's from 2014.

I don't care for this at all. The story wasn't very coherent, there was no real reason to care about what happened, and the creature itself was fine but not particularly memorable. -1

Also, Zulu is a language, Bantu is the language family. It's like saying "in the Romance language, spoken by the Romanian people."

An amount of black, viscous saliva containing various amounts of organic material from all previously consumed corpses was left on containment chamber walls, along with what appeared to be an intact traditional black Zulu dress.

An amount of black, viscous saliva containing various amounts of organic material from all previously consumed corpses was left on containment chamber walls, along with what appeared to be an intact traditional black Zulu dress.1

Footnotes
1. Thorough analysis of this material revealed significant titres of a heavily modified variant strain of SCP-742. Additional analysis of genetic material, including the accompanying viral particles, showed significant splicing and incorporation of functional genes from a variety of plants, and several scavenger species, aligning with genetic analysis of recovered samples of SCP-3140.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Upon finding a cadaver, SCP-550 will unravel itself to create a wide split in the area where a chest would be, and will kneel over and make contact with the cadaver. This cavity does not appear to be different from SCP-550's exterior, and it secretes high concentrations of hydrochloric acid.

The hydrochloric acid it produces is used in breaking down organic substances located in corpses, allowing it take in nutrients through pores in the wood it is composed of.

This is pretty much what it does. I can rephrase it a bit, I think.

Several ritualistic items such as incense and candles, along with pieces of a large cloth and various salts and spices were found scattered throughout the graveyard.

Hint, for why there's a tongue. I changed it from a quilt and just various spices to the bolded area.

And no, the cult was not responsible in screwing the guy up. They were trying to help the guy, though mostly for personal gain. I don't think anyone else ever would want what they wanted to happen to themselves (another hint: they're dead). I would prefer to leave the curling up part in, since I think the Foundation would come to that conclusion with all the background info.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm a little confused by this, so let me try and spell it out. Correct me if I'm wrong:

  • Skip is a humanoid made out of ash shavings.
  • It eats corpses. The method for how it does this was the most confusing part of the article.
  • The person who used to be this thing escaped some African cult that likely put some kind of spirit/monster/demon in them, for the express purpose of being consumed by it.
  • Person didn't jive with this, so they escaped to England and have been trying to contain themselves until something awoke the demon.
  • I don't know where the tongue thing fits in narratively, but I liked it. The description could use some serious cleanup, as could much of this article, and if you took out the bit about why it curled up afterward, you'd be showing a lot more.

So is this an original article with new stuff, an original article rewritten, or a completely new article?

Unrelated: "Fraxinus excelsior" is the most badass binomial nomenclature I think I've ever seen.

Neutral vote. I have no technical issues with how this was written, and it makes total sense that the Foundation would contain stuff like this. However, thematically speaking I feel like there's a lot of disparate elements to this thing, and the phone message is a little too cryptic in my estimation to really add much to the overall story.

Definitely an improvement, which I am all in favor of for Series I slots, but not really my personal cup of tea.
